title: Pharaoh's hard heart (Exodus 8–10)
hookLine: each time he relents, then hardens; the rabbis say a heart can harden by habit
last: TEN WAYS TO SAY LET GO.

lines: THE PROMISE MADE IN A CRISIS.
PRAY FOR ME, I'LL LET THEM GO.
cards: Some people can't back down. The argument is lost, everyone can see it, and still: no. Or the promise to change, made in the middle of a crisis, gone the moment things calm down.
Frogs are everywhere, in Pharaoh's bed, in his ovens. He calls Moses in a panic: pray for me, take them away, and I'll let the people go. Moses prays, and the frogs die.
And the text says: when Pharaoh saw there was relief, he hardened his heart.

teach.b: Read the plagues closely and you'll notice a pattern in the language.

teach.h: AT THE BOILS: GOD HARDENED IT.
teach.b: In the early plagues, the Torah says Pharaoh's heart was hardened, or Pharaoh hardened his heart. No one else is named as doing it. After the blood: "and Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he hearkened not unto them."

After the frogs, the lice, the swarms, the pestilence: the same. Then, at the sixth plague, the boils, the language turns: "And the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh." From then on, it's mostly God who hardens it.
That's troubling. If God hardened his heart, was Pharaoh still choosing? The rabbis argued about it, and gave different answers.
Maimonides said Pharaoh sinned freely at first, so badly and so often that he lost the path back: the door of turning closed, as a consequence of his own choices.
Sforno, a later Italian commentator, said nearly the opposite: God strengthened Pharaoh's heart so he could choose freely, and not just give in because of the pain.
Either way, notice the first five times: the text names no one forcing him.
Pirkei Avot, the sayings of the fathers, has a line that fits: one wrong deed drags another after it. Every time he said no, the next no came easier.
Hebrew uses three words for this hardening: chazak, strong, the same word as chazak at the end of Genesis; kaved, heavy; and kasheh, hard. A heart can get strong in the wrong way, heavy, stiff.
The rabbis' lesson is simple and a little scary: hearts harden by habit.

how: Jewish tradition uses Pharaoh's hardening to teach about teshuvah, turning back, and about how small repeated choices shape character; Pirkei Avot, the sayings of the fathers, is often studied on Shabbat afternoons.

o: heart: where you think and choose, not only feel
anger: the heat that rises in a stubborn person
courage: the strength to stand firm and not bend

games.q: what's inside the hardening — tap the pairs.
p: where God begins to harden it

s: from the very first plague, the Torah says God hardened Pharaoh's heart
in the first five plagues it says Pharaoh hardened his heart, or it was hardened.
the rabbis all agree on why God hardened his heart
Maimonides and Sforno give different answers.
Pharaoh promised to let the people go during the frogs
then, when there was relief, he hardened his heart.

games.q: you're Pharaoh. the frogs are gone. yesterday you promised to let the people go. what do you do?
o: change your mind now that it's over.
ask for one more day to think.
games.why: when he saw there was relief, he hardened his heart. the promise was gone as soon as the frogs were.

practice: Think of a position you keep repeating, with a person or an idea, mostly because you've always said it: a grudge, an I'll never, an old argument with a family member.
Put your hand on your chest if you like, and ask: is this still true, or just a habit? You don't have to give it up; just loosen your grip a little.

wordCard.voice: Lev, Hebrew for heart, the place of thought and choice, not only feeling. He promises, then hardens, again and again, until the hardening becomes who he is.

orig.note: Hebrew: heart. in the Bible, the heart is where you think and choose, not only where you feel.

carryVoice: Your line: hearts harden by habit. Small choices, repeated, shape a heart. Eighty-six days, and counting.
